title.narrative: Increasing resilience to the health risks of climate change in the Federated States of Micronesia

description.narrative:
The project will transform the current situation of high vulnerability to VBD, WBD and FBD risks related to climate change by developing a climate-resilient health system, as outlined in the NCCHAP, and implementing tangible human health adaptation activities at the community level. The project is organized around three components that are presented in the theory of change below (Figure 3).
The different activities have been developed taking into account recommendations from the NCCHAP and the joint external evaluation of International Health Regulations core capacities of FSM from the World Health Organization (WHO)[1] [about:blank].
Figure 3: Theory of Change
[https://formioblob.blob.core.windows.net/formio/uploads/image7-c4688cfc-4a61-40a2-b56c-8910d7cca31c.png?st=2020-11-24T04%3A06%3A38Z&se=2021-11-24T05%3A46%3A38Z&sp=r&sv=2018-03-28&sr=b&sig=S0Ka0xAjAMO%2BiEdR%2FxHl2YQ%2FgROD8Zt8enj7Ozx951Q%3D]
Component 1: Enabling environment
Expected outcome: Enhanced policies, capacities and cross-sectoral collaboration to mainstream and manage climate-sensitive health risks associated with VBD, WBD and FBD.
Activities:
1. Revise or update climate change and VBD, WBD and FBD policies and programs, including the NCCHAP, to better consider the extent to which climate variability and change could affect the spatial and temporal distribution of disease or could increase the numbers of injuries, illnesses, and deaths, and update action plans. In particular:
· on VBD, improve State’s vector management programs and animal surveillance;
· on water-borne diarrheal pathogens, expand the existing programs to outer islands, improve water safety planning for the four different states and review each state’s Rural Sanitation Program; and,
· on FBD, set official standards for food safety/handling (commercial, household).
2. Establish coordination mechanisms and memoranda of understanding between health-related Departments and agencies (e.g. those responsible for public health, water, waste management, food safety standards etc.) at the national and state levels to improve preventive and adaptive measures to climate-sensitive health risks including Standard Operating Procedures defining roles and responsibilities for inter-agency cooperation and collaboration to respond to climate-induced disease outbreaks;
3. Conduct trainings of the health workforce and technical officers in other Departments and organizations to manage climate-sensitive health outcomes on VBD, WBD and FBD (i.e. food safety officers, laboratory analysts).
Component 2: Harmonized climate and health information systems
Expected outcome: Improved surveillance of vector-, water- and food-borne diseases through harmonized climate and health information and early warning systems (HIEWS).
Activities:
1. Put in place a robust national climate-sensitive disease information system (for VBD, WBD and FBD) by applying modern mosquito surveillance and health data base management techniques based on digitized medical records and eHealth, with information overlaid with hydro-meteorological, sectoral, and spatial data;
2. Establish a national harmonized health-climate surveillance and early warning system for VBD, WBD and FBD; utilize the HIEWS to standardize information sharing at all levels of government and make it available to the Pacific Public Health Surveillance Network (PPHSN)[2] [about:blank], that will serve as a knowledge sharing platform for the Pacific region;
3. Conduct trainings of health professionals on data compilation, input and utilization of the HIEWS.
Component 3: Adaptation interventions at the community level to better cope with vector-, water- and food-borne diseases
Expected outcome: Increased resilience of most vulnerable communities to vector-, water- and food-borne diseases as the main climate-sensitive health risks.
Activities:
1. Assess community needs, risks areas, and improve health service delivery: conduct regular visits by health services personnel to selected high-risk communities to assess community needs and deliver effective prevention, management, and control of climate-related diseases particularly in areas or during periods in which there is an elevated risk as indicated by the HIEWS.
2. Produce, consolidate and disseminate awareness and prevention materials:
· Run public awareness campaigns through community meetings, radio programs, short videos and social media posts as well as posters and brochures to inform communities of potential climate health risks and precautions to take associated with VBD, WBD and FBD (e.g. education campaigns utilizing community leaders, youth and women in particular as agents of change, teaching about safe practices such as traditional food preparation techniques, food handling, pooled water around the home etc.).
· Provide tailored training to vulnerable communities on how to interpret messages disseminated through the HIEWS including on recommended actions to take in relation to specific advisories on climate-induced outbreaks of various VBD, WBD and FBD.
· On VBD, identify and manage high-risk mosquito breeding sites using GIS mapping, distribute mosquito nets and conduct environmental clean-ups, using vector control interventions.
· On WBD, improve year-round access to climate-resilient, safe and reliable drinking water supply through the installation of climate-resilient rainwater tanks at the household level, distribution of water sanitizing tablets and distribution of household test kits.
· On FBD, improve the diagnostic capacity of the FSM Food Safety Laboratory and ensure it is fully stocked with necessary equipment and consumables. Increase capacity and quality control and assurance of the laboratory to provide better food safety testing and public guidelines on climate-related food borne diseases.
3. Train health workforce and technical officers to manage climate-sensitive disease: conduct trainings for local health officers to better support communities to cope with climate-induced health risks associated with VBD, WBD and FBD through responding to climate-induced disease outbreaks at the local level as per the Standard Operating Procedures, feeding data into and interpreting data from the climate-sensitive disease information system and HIEWS, and supporting communities to implement preventive measures as well as take action in response to advisories disseminated by the HIEWS.
To date, health risks associated with climate change impacts have been dealt with as co-benefits of sectoral or integrated interventions such as water management, disaster-risk reduction etc. For instance, several climate change adaptation and water security projects have been and are being implemented in FSM with expected benefits on health (such as the RENI project implemented by SPC and the Adaptation Fund’s “Enhancing the climate resilience of vulnerable island communities” project implemented by SPREP). Since all the previous and current projects are mainly focused on food and water security[3] [about:blank], food and water safety have not been yet tackled on a large scale. On prevention of VBDs, some work has been conducted in the states (mapping exercise on areas prone to mosquito breeding sites, mosquito spraying activities and awareness flyers to support the prevention of dengue fever in Kosrae, municipal solid waste sanitation programs to remove waste that could be potential breeding sites for vectors in Pohnpei). These activities have the potential to be scaled up and to use GIS and other new scientific technologies to maximize their impacts.
This project is building on such initiatives but with an entirely dedicated focus on climate-sensitive health risks (VBD, WBD and FBD) with an objective towards transformational impact through policy changes (with subsequent changes in planning and practices), integrated information and surveillance systems and adaptation interventions at all level (national, States, communities). As a SAP project, this project is directed to a specific, targeted few communities that will be selected due to certain criteria including their past outbreaks, susceptibility to future outbreaks (e.g. poor water and sanitation infrastructure), vulnerability to climate change impacts (coastal and rural communities) and with the perspective to target a set of diverse communities, noting ease of access as one factor, to trial this project. This project is meant to be scalable in FSM, and later throughout the Pacific. Targeted communities will reflect 20% of the FSM population (approximately 3,500 households).
The proposed interventions will contribute to reducing the risk of climate-sensitive diseases for most vulnerable communities and reduced health costs as a result of improved access to clean drinking water, food safety and vector control.The new harmonized health information system has the potential to be transformational with its use as an early warning detection for outbreaks. State departments of Health and EPA offices will be the major implementing agencies for the community interventions. In addition, the long-term sustainability of the programme will be ensured by empowering communities to maintain and manage their assets into the future. A detailed cost benefit analysis will be undertaken when developing the funding proposal.
The Pacific Community (SPC) will be the Accredidted Entity for this project. SPC’s comparative advantage lies in:
1) Its extensive ties with Pacific Islands governments, administrations, agencies and partners in all Pacific island countries, and especially in FSM through its regional office.
2) Its broad mandate on development issues – inter alia health, fisheries, energy and transport, water, climate change and environmental sustainability, gender in development, human rights and natural resource management.
3) Its large funding base with multi-lateral and bilateral donors, allowing for cofinancing options, cost sharing and combined programmatic funding.
4) A strong and solid experience in project management and delivery, and diligent independent project evaluations.
5) Its extensive international partnerships which range from UN agencies to other IGOs, NGOs, civil society groups, the informal sector etc. As a result, SPC is able to generate project impacts from the highest level right down to the grassroots level in communities.
The implementation arrangement for the project will include a close collaboration between the SPC Public Health Division (PHD), which is the focal point of the Pacific Public Health Surveillance Network, and the FSM Department of Health & Social Affairs (DHSA). The DHSA will serve as the main Executing Entitiy (EE) for the project, with the Project Management Unit (PMU) housed within the Department, overseen by a Program Manager (the current Manager of the Environmental Health and Preparedness Unit). A national project manager, administrative/finance officer, procurement officer, four state coordinators and four support staff will support day-to-day execution of the project. At the same time, SPC-PHD will provide technical support to the project activities as an EE, and house part of the PMU, with overall supervision from the SPC Climate Change and Environmental Sustainability (CCES) division, and headed up by a Project Advisor, and a Finance and Contract Specialist at the SPC North Pacific Regional Office. The PMU will ensure appropriate contract and fiduciary management and reporting to GCF, provision of technical assistance and training, environmental and social safeguards, as well as due diligence and accountability. Both of the organizations shall work together with the various national and state agencies and implementating partners, and shall report to and be guided by a National Steering Committee (NSC). The NSC will be comprised of all required FSM Departments, as well as an appointed representative from each fo the four FSM states, and one representative from SPC. A major aim of this arrangement will be to reinforce the country-driven approach. The project will seek to build institutional, systemic and individual capacities within the nation, with a particular focus on establishing/strengthening the Environmental Health Units in each of the jurisdictions, focusing on the programs of VDB, WBD and FBD detection, prevention and control. This will facilitate long-term sustainability of the GCF-funded inititative.
[https://formioblob.blob.core.windows.net/formio/uploads/image8-93535140-9277-4b95-813b-66724d5cb29a.png?st=2020-11-24T04%3A07%3A28Z&se=2021-11-24T05%3A47%3A28Z&sp=r&sv=2018-03-28&sr=b&sig=wgVnRfbVt2%2FbPZTfXnn1bV1HbGQjGM21YZDBpgVJ4yk%3D]
Figure 4: Project Implementation Arrangements
Risks associated with this project are relatively low and relate mainly to natural hazards that can damage or incapacitate the health system or prevent communities from engaging in the project. As this risk cannot be eliminated, weather forecasts will be monitored and necessary adaptation measures will be taken in case of natural disaster.
Instability in targeted communities, such as conflict or a change of leadership could lead to delays or unwillingness to engage with component 3 of the project. However, this can be mitigated by maintaining strong relationships and good communications with local municipalities so that the engagement approach can be adapted.
A loss of political will might also slow down the implementation of the project, especially regarding the first component. However, this risk remains relatively low since both national and states governments perceive VBD, WBD and FBD as major threats for the future well-being of their constituencies. This risk will be mitigated through ongoing cooperation and communication with stakeholders at national and state level.
A full risk analysis will be outlined in the full proposal.
A consultative process initiated at an inception workshop will identify MEL indicators relevant for the project that will include clearly formulated goals, objectives, and measures. MEL oversight and monitoring responsibilities will be led by the Project Advisor (SPC) with input from the FSM national Project Manager (DHSA) and the national Steering Committee designated to assess project performance. The Steering Committee will assess progress on an annual basis, using the chosen indicators, and will review the annual work plan for the subsequent year, suggesting mid-course corrections as needed. These will be documented in an annual report. A mid-term and terminal evaluation will assess progress, with the mid-term evaluation recommending any corrective actions needed to ensure the project achieves the desired outcomes. An end-of-project review will capture lessons learned and best practices that will be described in the final report and outreach materials for relevant audiences.
